issues.title: Transient threshold uses a product instead of a reciprocal
issues.failure_explanation: The old display claims that the actual norm at the simulated crossing time is 0.5 degrees Celsius multiplied by 1+xi. The preceding ratio and the condition that the simulated norm equals 0.5 degrees Celsius instead establish 0.5 divided by 1+xi. The two expressions differ whenever xi is nonzero and reverse the dependence on the norm ratio.
issues.overall_effect: The displayed relation misstates the actual transient magnitude at the simulated threshold and contradicts the numerical discussion, although no formal result depends on it.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the displayed product 0.5 degrees Celsius · (1+ξ(tilde t*)) with the quotient 0.5 degrees Celsius/(1+ξ(tilde t*)).
issues.why_classification: The preceding norm ratio and the simulated-threshold equation uniquely force the quotient, and the surrounding numerical discussion already follows that reading. An intended reader can make the correction directly without repairing any argument or dependent result.

issues.title: Componentwise consequence names the initial error instead of the solution error

failure_location.quote: if the normwise relative error $\delta(t)$ is small, then the componentwise relative error $\varepsilon_\ell$ is small for components $y_\ell(t)$ with a non-large ratio $\frac{\Vert y(t)\Vert}{\vert y_\ell(t)\vert}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The old prose claims that a small normwise solution error delta(t) implies a small initial componentwise error epsilon_l. The displayed inequality actually establishes an upper bound for the solution componentwise error delta_l(t), subject to the component-to-norm ratio. Thus the old assertion names a different error at a different time from the quantity supported by item 3.
issues.overall_effect: The local guidance about extracting componentwise information from the normwise error identifies the wrong quantity; the displayed inequality itself remains correct.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In item 3', replace the initial componentwise error ε_l with the solution componentwise error δ_l(t).
issues.why_classification: The displayed inequality, the reference to δ(t), and the components y_l(t) uniquely identify δ_l(t) as the intended quantity. This is a single misnamed symbol, with no mathematical inference or dependent statement requiring repair.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: In particular, point 3) is useful for estimating the order of magnitude of $\delta_l(t)$, once the order of magnitude of $\delta(t)$ is known

issues.title: Complex-onset example inserts an extra square root
issues.failure_explanation: The old example claims that the contribution inherited from epsilonc< is one half times log of 1 over the square root of 1-V1, yielding 1.6844. The cited old bound actually contains one half times log of 1 over 1-V1. Since taking the square root already contributes another factor of one half to the logarithm, the displayed numerical contribution is too small by a factor of two.
issues.overall_effect: The illustrative numerical assessment understates the complex-onset delay contribution, but the governing bound epsilonc< is correct and no formal result is affected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace (1/2)log(1/sqrt(1−V₁)) with (1/2)log(1/(1−V₁)), recompute the displayed contribution as approximately 3.3688 rather than 1.6844, and adjust the adjoining illustrative onset assessment accordingly.
issues.why_classification: The governing bound is correct, and the example is repaired by a short, routine substitution and numerical recomputation with no effect on any formal result. It exceeds a typo because the reported number was actually calculated from the erroneous extra square root, so the numerical assessment depended on the wrong expression.

issues.title: Real-eigenvalue identity uses the Euclidean norm under a general p-norm
issues.failure_explanation: Because the old definition is hat y0=y0 divided by the active vector norm, the reciprocal inner-product identity equals ||w^(1)|| times the active norm of y0 divided by |w^(1)y0|. The old formula instead uses ||y0||_2, which is generally different for p=1 and p=infinity, so the displayed equality is false outside the Euclidean case.
issues.overall_effect: The exact characterization accompanying the empirical real-eigenvalue comparison is wrong for the 1- and infinity-norm cases; the Euclidean case is unaffected.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In the identity tagged KandK+, replace ||y₀||₂ with ||y₀||, where ||·|| is the active p-norm used to define the normalized initial value.
issues.why_classification: From hat y₀=y₀/||y₀|| and the first expression 1/|hat w^(1) hat y₀|, the active norm ||y₀|| is algebraically and uniquely forced. Removing the Euclidean subscript restores the intended identity for all stated p-norms without changing any inference or dependent result.
